Print a Model-Comparison Table

Source: R/wrapper.R
print.mixture_comparison.Rd

Prints the table compare_mixtures() and compare_longitudinal() return. The default view keeps the columns with the strongest record for choosing the number of classes, so the table fits one screen: the log-likelihood and parameter count, BIC (the best-supported information criterion in the simulations of Nylund, Asparouhov & Muthen, 2007), SABIC (better than BIC for categorical indicators at smaller samples, same source), AIC3 (strong for latent class models with categorical indicators; Dias, 2006), Entropy (classification quality, not a criterion for K; Masyn, 2013) and the VLMR p-values when they were requested. columns = "all" adds AIC, CAIC, AWE, ICL, BF and cmP, the full table of Masyn (2013). Nothing is dropped from x$fit_table, which keeps every column at full precision.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mixture_comparison'
print(x, columns = c("default", "all"), ...)

Arguments

x

A mixture_comparison object.

columns

"default" for the short table, "all" for every column.

...

Ignored.

Value

x, invisibly.

Details

AWE and cmP are left out of the default view on purpose. In a large simulation that included misspecified models, Arch and Nylund-Gibson (2026) found BIC and CAIC the most reliable indices, with no significant difference between the two; AWE performed worst overall, most of all at small samples; and cmP, being a rescaling of the BIC differences in the table, tracked BIC so closely that printing it adds no independent evidence and can make one index's choice look like two. The classes in every simulated population were well separated (entropy about .84 to .88), so the ranking is firmest there.

A log-likelihood marked * is a maximum that only one start reached. BF spans many orders of magnitude, and its reading bands stop at 100 and start at 0.1 (Wagenmakers, 2007), so it is printed as > 100 and < 0.1 beyond them; cmP below 0.001 is printed as < 0.001.

References

Arch, D. A. N., & Nylund-Gibson, K. (2026). Unmodeled DIF in latent class analysis: Consequences for class enumeration. Methods in Psychology, 14, 100243. doi:10.1016/j.metip.2026.100243

Dias, J. G. (2006). Latent class analysis and model selection. In M. Spiliopoulou et al. (Eds.), From Data and Information Analysis to Knowledge Engineering (pp. 95-102). Springer.

Masyn, K. E. (2013). Latent class analysis and finite mixture modeling. In T. D. Little (Ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Quantitative Methods (Vol. 2, pp. 551-611). Oxford University Press.

Nylund, K. L., Asparouhov, T., & Muthen, B. O. (2007). Deciding on the number of classes in latent class analysis and growth mixture modeling: A Monte Carlo simulation study. Structural Equation Modeling, 14(4), 535-569. doi:10.1080/10705510701575396

Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2007). A practical solution to the pervasive problems of p values. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14(5), 779-804. doi:10.3758/BF03194105
